article_title: Affordance-Based Approach to Language Assessment
citation: Quang Nhat Nguyen & Dung Thi Hue Doan. (2025). Affordance-based Approach to Language Assessment. Language Education & Assessment, 8(1). https://doi.org/10.29140/lea.v8n1.103000
title: Affordance-based assessment should complement, not replace, outcome-based assessment
description: The paper explicitly states that an affordance perspective does not reject outcome-based assessments outright: standardized or outcome-oriented tasks remain useful for benchmarking and accountability. The affordance-based view instead reframes priorities, urging educators to look beyond test scores and consider how learners engage with and expand the opportunities before them, positioning assessment as both evaluative and generative.
requirements: Educators retain outcome-based tasks for benchmarking and accountability while adding ecological documentation
constraints: Affordance-based approaches risk inconsistency across cohorts, higher teacher workload, and difficulty ensuring reliability without a strong rubric and training
examples: Table 1 contrasts outcome-based methods such as a 90-minute closed-book end-of-term writing exam with affordance-based methods such as a semester-long portfolio of drafts, peer feedback, and self-reflection.
key_sources: Quang Nhat Nguyen & Dung Thi Hue Doan. (2025). Affordance-based Approach to Language Assessment. Language Education & Assessment, 8(1). https://doi.org/10.29140/lea.v8n1.103000

article_title: If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover
citation: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://edtrust.org
title: Affirm teachers' humanity and racial identity so teachers of color can be their authentic selves at school
description: Case-study principals deliberately create space for teachers to be themselves as individuals and as people of color, including freedom in dress, hair, and cultural expression. Teachers described being able to wear culturally affirming clothing and wear natural hair, and one school ran a building-wide "Woke Wednesdays" initiative demonstrating "their commitment to consciousness and social justice." Administrators of color were noted as making teachers feel safer and heard.
requirements: Administrative support, including administrators of color, so teachers do not feel they must leave their identity at the school door.
examples: Teachers wore shirts such as "I'm Rooting for Everybody Black" without reprisal; a leader transitioning to dreadlocks felt comfortable not hiding her hair under a wig.
key_sources: Davis Dixon, Ashley Griffin, and Mark Teoh. (2019). If You Listen, We Will Stay: Why Teachers of Color Leave and How to Disrupt Teacher Turnover. The Education Trust & Teach Plus. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED603193

article_title: From digital competence to AI-responsive pedagogy: a scoping review of technology-supported teacher education
citation: Patiño Hernández JF, Chiappe A and Ortega González E (2026). From digital competence to AI-responsive pedagogy: a scoping review of technology-supported teacher education. Front. Educ. 11:1949296. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1949296
title: Technological affordances become educationally meaningful only when mediated by pedagogical design, professional judgement and institutional support
description: Across both evidence streams, the review concludes that technology's value in teacher education depends on conditions beyond the tool itself. The synthesis states that "technological affordances became educationally meaningful when mediated by pedagogical design, disciplinary knowledge, critical and ethical judgement, human oversight, professional agency, and institutional support". This principle supports an approach to teacher education emphasising pedagogically justified and professionally accountable AI use rather than tool adoption alone.
requirements: Pedagogical design, disciplinary knowledge, critical and ethical judgement, human oversight, professional agency and institutional support
constraints: The recurrent strategy-advantage-barrier configurations are descriptive co-classifications within the reviewed corpus and do not imply that a strategy caused the associated advantage or barrier
target_learning_goals: pedagogically justified technology and AI integration
sustained professional learning and transfer to practice
examples: The review's cross-category synthesis linked competence-framework strategies mainly to digital competence gains, while barriers concentrated on infrastructure, transfer and preparation.
key_sources: Patiño Hernández JF, Chiappe A and Ortega González E (2026). From digital competence to AI-responsive pedagogy: a scoping review of technology-supported teacher education. Front. Educ. 11:1949296. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1949296

article_title: An Interpretable Closed-Loop Intelligent Tutoring System for Multimodal Affective Feedback in Asynchronous Presentation Training
citation: Hung-Yue Suen and Kuo-En Hung. (2026). An Interpretable Closed-Loop Intelligent Tutoring System for Multimodal Affective Feedback in Asynchronous Presentation Training. IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1109/TLT.2026.3693864
title: Treat affective signals as audience-perceivable expressive behaviors, not evidence of internal emotional states
description: In the system's expressive diagnosis layer, affective signals are explicitly not designed to capture the speaker's internal emotional states; instead they capture "expressive cues that are perceivable by an audience and that shape how the presentation is received," consistent with observer-based affect perception research. Facial expressions support interpretation of Nonverbal Expressiveness, vocal and verbal expressions support Voice & Talk, and lexical expressions contextualize Topic, Content, and Clarity. This framing keeps emotion analytics pedagogically interpretable and tied to the rubric.
requirements: Emotion probabilities normalized per video and presented as descriptive information linked to BARS dimensions
constraints: Cues are treated as behavioral signals providing interpretable information about delivery, not as direct evidence of internal states
target_learning_goals: understanding why specific presentation dimensions underperform and adjusting expressive delivery
examples: The dashboard presents segment-level facial and vocal emotion distributions over six basic emotions and a valence–arousal lexical analysis with four affective orientations, letting learners click slices to review representative video or audio segments.
key_sources: Hung-Yue Suen and Kuo-En Hung. (2026). An Interpretable Closed-Loop Intelligent Tutoring System for Multimodal Affective Feedback in Asynchronous Presentation Training. IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies. https://doi.org/10.1109/TLT.2026.3693864

article_title: Can You Feel It? A Practical Guide to Emotional Micro-Interventions for Higher Education Teachers
citation: François PARLANT. (2025). Can You Feel It? A Practical Guide to Emotional Micro-Interventions for Higher Education Teachers (and Others). https://osf.io/tuw2a/overview
title: Affective Pedagogical Content Knowledge (APCK): an extension of PCK integrating content, student difficulties, and affective-strategic knowledge
description: The article proposes APCK as a specialized extension of Shulman's Pedagogical Content Knowledge for affectively charged domains. It "integrates three knowledge bases": content mastery, knowledge of common conceptual and emotional bottlenecks, and "Affective-Strategic Knowledge: A repertoire of verbal and non-verbal strategies (micro-interventions) designed to navigate those emotional bottlenecks while advancing content learning." The guide metaphor (content expert, group dynamist, logistical scout) embodies APCK in action.
requirements: Requires the instructor to synthesize knowledge of the terrain (content), the travelers (students), and the journey (learning process) for moment-by-moment decisions
constraints: The article states the evidence for the framework is anecdotal and qualitative, drawn from reflective practice
target_learners: Higher education students in skill-based disciplines
target_learning_goals: Student resilience, self-efficacy, and engagement in high-stakes learning
examples: The expert guide is not just a historian (content expert) but also a Group Dynamist who reads morale and a Logistical Scout who anticipates pitfalls and prepares remedies
key_sources: François PARLANT. (2025). Can You Feel It? A Practical Guide to Emotional Micro-Interventions for Higher Education Teachers (and Others). https://osf.io/tuw2a/overview

article_title: (In)equitable Schooling and Mathematics of Marginalized Students: Through the Voices of Urban Latinas/os
citation: Maura Varley Gutiérrez, Craig Willey, & Lena L. Khisty. (2011). (In)equitable Schooling and Mathematics of Marginalized Students: Through the Voices of Urban Latinas/os. Journal of Urban Mathematics Education, 4(2), 26–43. http://education.gsu.edu/JUME
title: After-school mathematics clubs as counter spaces using home language, community, and knowledge as learning resources
description: The after-school mathematics clubs were designed as alternative learning environments that 'explicitly defined and utilized students' home language, communities, and knowledge as learning resources.' They offered collaborative, project-based activities with cross-generational participants (students, preservice teachers, researchers), and became counter spaces that naturally provoked students to compare, analyze, question, and comment on their mathematics experiences in both settings.
requirements: Activities must value and integrate students' language, experiences, and communities; adults often spoke in Spanish and tasks were written in two languages
constraints: Students volunteered to participate; the clubs ran 8 to 12 weeks each school semester, meeting approximately two hours once or twice a week
target_learners: Third- to sixth-grade urban Latina/o students with a range of Spanish and English proficiencies
target_learning_goals: More advanced mathematics opportunities and practices than students typically received in their regular classes
examples: Approximately 34 students across a Midwestern dual-language site and a Southwestern site participated, many for all three years
key_sources: Maura Varley Gutiérrez, Craig Willey, & Lena L. Khisty. (2011). (In)equitable Schooling and Mathematics of Marginalized Students: Through the Voices of Urban Latinas/os. Journal of Urban Mathematics Education, 4(2), 26–43. http://education.gsu.edu/JUME

article_title: Using a computer simulation for teaching communication skills: A blinded multisite mixed methods randomized controlled trial
citation: Kron Frederick W. MD, Fetters Michael D. MD, MPH, MA, Scerbo Mark W. PhD, White Casey B. PhD, Lypson Monica L. MD, MHPE, FACP, Padilla Miguel A. PhD, Gliva-McConvey Gayle A., Belfore Lee A. II PhD, West Temple MPA, Wallace Amelia M. BM, Guetterman Timothy C. PhD, Schleicher Lauren S. MA, Kennedy Rebecca A. MS, Mangrulkar Rajesh S. MD, Cleary James F. MD, Marsella Stacy C. PhD, Becker Daniel M. MD. (2017). Using a computer simulation for teaching communication skills: A blinded multisite mixed methods randomized controlled trial. Patient Education and Counseling. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pec.2016.10.024
title: Pair scenario practice with an after-action review giving general-principles feedback, then a second run-through, to deepen learning and support transfer
description: The article's design gives learners an initial scenario run-through, a personalized after-action review (AAR), and a second run-through to apply what they learned. The AAR presents "the evidence behind specific verbal choices, the consequences of the choices, and offering suggestions for improvement" without marking answers correct or incorrect, and addresses general principles of effective communication rather than specific choices, because general information facilitates deeper learning and transfer.
requirements: A scenario that can be run through twice with recorded performance, personalized feedback available immediately after the first run-through, and feedback framed around general communication principles rather than item-by-item correctness.
constraints: The article states the OSCE transfer scenario was a successive approximation closer to, but not an actual clinical setting; validating transfer to real patient encounters remains future research.
target_learning_goals: Applying communication feedback in a repeat interaction
Reflective learning on verbal and nonverbal choices
Transfer of communication skills to novel scenarios
examples: MPathic-VR students viewed video of their own nonverbal behaviors in the AAR, received feedback on detected behaviors such as nodding and smiling, and then completed a second run-through of each scenario.

MD, Cleary James F. MD, Marsella Stacy C. PhD, Becker Daniel M. MD. (2017). Using a computer simulation for teaching communication skills: A blinded multisite mixed methods randomized controlled trial. Patient Education and Counseling. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pec.2016.10.024

article_title: Classical dialogs in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Classical dialogs in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9071-y
title: Affordances of artifacts are not fully predefined by the technology but depend on established practices consolidated in body schemas or habitus
description: Drawing on Dohn's Merleau-Pontian analysis, the editorial states that "the 'affordances' of an artifact are not fully predefined by the technology" and that affordances of Web 2.0 technologies "depend on our established practices as consolidated in our body schemas (Merleau-Ponty) or habitus (Bourdieu)." This explains why the same tool is enacted differently across situated practices.
requirements: Analysis of technology affordances must attend to users' established practices and embodied dispositions
constraints: Conventional educational structures — grading, instruction traditions, individual-outcome focus — militate against Web 2.0 goals of collective wisdom and social networking
target_learners: University students using Web 2.0 technologies in courses
target_learning_goals: Participating in collective knowledge practices with social technologies
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Classical dialogs in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9071-y

article_title: Consistent practices in artifact-mediated collaboration
citation: Nathan Dwyer & Daniel D. Suthers. (2006). Consistent practices in artifact-mediated collaboration. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 1: 481–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-006-9001-1
title: Invariants of artifact-mediated collaboration as a basis for abstract design models connecting representational affordances to communicative functions
description: The article proposes that the observed invariants — consistent communicative functions enacted across different media, participants and topics — can form "the basis for user-interface design principles" for collaborative software. The model would connect representational affordances (reorientability, repositionability, space, attachability) to the communicative functions pairs consistently accomplish (awareness management, relatedness, grouping, functional spaces). The authors present it as "a promising first step towards creating an abstract model for design" and note some invariants "challenge common HCI design wisdom." It derives from qualitative observation of six pairs, not from testing designed interfaces.
requirements: Design must tolerate flexible, context-derived meanings rather than rigid GUI mappings between interface elements and functionality
constraints: Derived from short, synchronous, handwriting-limited sessions on wicked problems with no external data or formal evaluation criteria; the authors note a longer time frame might motivate more organizational mechanisms
target_learners: Pairs of students collaborating synchronously via shared written representations
target_learning_goals: Collaborative discussion, negotiation and joint agreement on open-ended problems
examples: Six pairs used paper office supplies (index cards, Post-It notes, large sheets) under a screen that hid faces, with silence required, while video captured the workspace
key_sources: Nathan Dwyer & Daniel D. Suthers. (2006). Consistent practices in artifact-mediated collaboration. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 1: 481–511. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-006-9001-1

article_title: Practice perspectives in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Practice perspectives in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9065-9
title: Affordances are enacted by user practices, not objective properties of artifacts
description: Following Dohn's article in the issue, affordances should not be treated as objective properties of artifacts independent of their users; they are relative to the 'interaction potential' of the people who see and use the artifacts, grounded in phenomenological accounts of embodiment. The editorial states: 'The affordances of the technologies are to be found not in the plans of the programmers or instructors, but in the practices of the users.'
requirements: Analysis of affordances must examine how user groups enact designed features and adapt their interaction practices
examples: In the VMT environment, affordances 'were determined in terms of the ways in which the user groups enacted the designed features and adapted their interaction practices to the technical environment'.
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Practice perspectives in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9065-9

article_title: From the Lab to the Wild: Examining Generalizability of Video-based Mind Wandering Detection
citation: Bühler, B., Bozkir, E., Goldberg, P., Sümer, Ö., D'Mello, S., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Kasneci, E. (2025). From the Lab to the Wild: Examining Generalizability of Video-based Mind Wandering Detection. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35, 823–857. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00412-2
title: Transfer-learning pipeline using AffectNet-pretrained ResNet50 latent features for video-based mind wandering detection
description: A detection pipeline in which the article uses transfer learning, where the feature extraction part of a ResNet50 CNN pre-trained on the AffectNet facial expression recognition dataset is applied to webcam video. Faces are detected frame-wise with RetinaFace, aligned, cropped, and fed to the CNN without its classification layer, producing a 2048-digit latent feature vector passed to downstream classifiers including SVMs, XGBoost, DNNs, and LSTM/BiLSTM temporal models, with an optional fine-tuned end-to-end CNN-LSTM variant.
requirements: Learner facial video from consumer-grade webcams with faces detectable across all frames; the article removed instances where no face could be detected across all frames
Ground-truth mind wandering self-reports (self-caught or probe-caught) for supervised training or evaluation
constraints: The in-the-wild dataset used for cross-dataset evaluation is modest in size (N = 15 participants), so it was used solely for evaluation purposes
target_learners: university students in online learning settings such as reading scientific text or watching video lectures
target_learning_goals: continuous, non-intrusive assessment of learners' attentional state (mind wandering) during learning tasks
examples: Within the lab study, latent features reached F1 up to 0.459 (LSTM); in cross-dataset prediction, BiLSTM on latent features reached F1 0.352, comparable to the state-of-the-art
key_sources: Bühler, B., Bozkir, E., Goldberg, P., Sümer, Ö., D'Mello, S., Gerjets, P., Trautwein, U., Kasneci, E. (2025). From the Lab to the Wild: Examining Generalizability of Video-based Mind Wandering Detection. Int J Artif Intell Educ 35, 823–857. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00412-2

article_title: Designing electronic collaborative learning environments
citation: Paul A. Kirschner, Jan Willem Strijbos, Karel Kreijns, Pieter Beers. (2004). Designing electronic collaborative learning environments. Educational Technology Research and Development, 52(3), pp.47-66. https://hal.science/hal-00703892
title: An affordance framework for electronic collaborative learning environments
description: The article presents what it calls an affordance framework for electronic collaborative learning environments for learning and working. The framework is offered as a shared lens because designers currently build such environments according to their own constructivist interpretations, educators employ them in diverse situations, and researchers comparing them find no conclusive evidence about whether, where, when or why they work. The framework is intended to structure the design and evaluation of these environments.
requirements: Applies to electronic collaborative learning environments used for learning and working
constraints: Motivated by the article's observation that researchers studying such environments find no conclusive evidence as to whether, where, when and why they work
target_learners: Students using electronic collaborative learning environments
examples: The article presents the framework alongside an interaction design procedure and an educational affordance approach to tasks, with results of three projects dealing with these three issues.
key_sources: Paul A. Kirschner, Jan Willem Strijbos, Karel Kreijns, Pieter Beers. (2004). Designing electronic collaborative learning environments. Educational Technology Research and Development, 52(3), pp.47-66. https://hal.science/hal-00703892

article_title: Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds
citation: Xining Wang, Gareth W. Young, Adéla Plechatá, Conor Mc Guckin, Guido Makransky. (2023). Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104815
title: Use affordable Cardboard VR solutions to bring immersive social competence education to under-resourced rural schools
description: The article recommends low-budget VR hardware as a route to social competence education in regions with limited resources. Cardboard VR is described as "a low-budget, easy assembly, and stereoscopic viewer that can be used with most smartphone devices", and the authors report that some children experienced discomfort despite the controller-free interaction. This made the intervention feasible in rural schools where field trips and advanced technology are unaffordable.
requirements: A smartphone and low-cost stereoscopic viewer; instructor-guided sessions
constraints: A few children reported discomfort with Cardboard VR; rural teachers may resist applying cutting-edge technology
target_learners: Rural children in underdeveloped countries and regions with limited educational resources
target_learning_goals: Social competence education and access to diverse educational experiences such as virtual museum visits
examples: The studies provided three device types (Cardboard VR, Meta Quest 2, Tablet VR) so children could experience different VR functions
key_sources: Xining Wang, Gareth W. Young, Adéla Plechatá, Conor Mc Guckin, Guido Makransky. (2023). Utilizing virtual reality to assist social competence education and social support for children from under-represented backgrounds. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104815

article_title: Nutritional Education in Medical Curricula and Clinical Practice: A Scoping Review on the Knowledge Deficit Amongst Medical Students and Doctors.
citation: Khiri Nasr and Kristy Howells. (2025). Nutritional Education in Medical Curricula and Clinical Practice: A Scoping Review on the Knowledge Deficit Amongst Medical Students and Doctors. Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics. https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.70031
title: AfN undergraduate nutrition curriculum for medical doctors: 13 core competencies assessed through 11 graduation criteria
description: The Association for Nutrition, with the Academy of Medical Royal Colleges and the General Medical Council, launched an initiative to incorporate nutrition into UK undergraduate medical curricula, in which "13 core nutritional competencies have been developed, which are assessed through 11 graduation criteria". Competencies span Knowledge, Assessment and Skills in Intervention, covering healthy balanced diets, ethical and legal considerations, nutritional status evaluation (e.g., BMI), and initiating sensitive nutrition conversations and referrals.
requirements: National standardisation and adoption by medical schools with graduation benchmarks
key_sources: Khiri Nasr and Kristy Howells. (2025). Nutritional Education in Medical Curricula and Clinical Practice: A Scoping Review on the Knowledge Deficit Amongst Medical Students and Doctors. Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics. https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.70031

article_title: Revisiting the trajectory of medical students' empathy, and impact of gender, specialty preferences and nationality: a systematic review.
citation: Andersen Freja Allerelli, Johansen Ann-Sofie Bering, Søndergaard Jens, Andersen Christina Maar, Assing Hvidt Elisabeth. (2020). Revisiting the trajectory of medical students' empathy, and impact of gender, specialty preferences and nationality: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-1964-5
title: Two-component taxonomy of empathy: affective and cognitive empathy
description: The review organises empathy as a construct with distinct components, stating that "Empathy is usually categorised as either affective (emotional), cognitive or a combination of both". Affective empathy is described as compassion and the ability to enter into other peoples' feelings, while cognitive empathy is the ability to understand someone's situation without making it one's own. In the clinical setting, the review states it is predominantly the cognitive empathy type that is valued and strived for. The review applies this distinction when interpreting studies, for example one cross-sectional study that differentiated between emotional and cognitive empathy and found higher cognitive empathy in final-year students.
requirements: Measurement instruments must distinguish the component being measured, since scales such as the BEES and TEQ measure affective empathy while the RMET measures cognitive empathy
constraints: The review notes that many different definitions and understandings of empathy, and different ways of measuring it, have led to ambiguous results
examples: One included cross-sectional study differentiated between emotional and cognitive empathy and found a higher cognitive empathy level in final year students compared to first-year students
key_sources: Andersen Freja Allerelli, Johansen Ann-Sofie Bering, Søndergaard Jens, Andersen Christina Maar, Assing Hvidt Elisabeth. (2020). Revisiting the trajectory of medical students' empathy, and impact of gender, specialty preferences and nationality: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-1964-5

article_title: The Application of Humorous Song in EFL Classrooms and Its Effects on Listening Comprehension
citation: Marzieh Rafiee, Zohre Kassaian, Hossein Vahid Dastjerdi. (2010). The Application of Humorous Song in EFL Classrooms and Its Effects on Listening Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 3(4). http://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Affective-environment approaches: Humanistic teaching and Suggestopedia frame humor and song as anxiety-reducing aids to language learning
description: The article situates humor and song within two approaches that prioritize a relaxed classroom atmosphere. Humanistic teaching "tries to secure a positive atmosphere before a learner begins an effort", with eradication of anxiety as a milestone. Suggestopedia uses "a relaxation session for unconscious assimilation of the lesson materials", in which music increases self-esteem and energizes learners. The study's humorous-song treatment is framed as an application of this affective perspective, chosen because the indirect, environment-focused perspective on humor has proven more fruitful in measurable effects.
requirements: Learners must feel secure and free of stress so they can focus on language tasks
constraints: The article focuses on the indirect effects of humor on the general classroom environment rather than direct effects on information retention
examples: The study played Shel Silverstein humorous songs after course-material listening across seventeen 90-minute sessions, with instructors asking no questions so students stayed relaxed.
key_sources: Marzieh Rafiee, Zohre Kassaian, Hossein Vahid Dastjerdi. (2010). The Application of Humorous Song in EFL Classrooms and Its Effects on Listening Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 3(4). http://www.ccsenet.org/elt

article_title: An After-School Intervention Targeting Executive Function and Visuospatial Skills Also Improves Classroom Behavior
citation: Laura L. Brock, William M. Murrah, Elizabeth A. Cottone, Andrew J. Mashburn, and David W. Grissmer. (2018). An after-school intervention targeting executive function and visuospatial skills also improves classroom behavior. International Journal of Behavioral Development, 42(5), 474–484. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025417738057
title: After-school EF/VS curriculum of constructional, paper-and-pencil, and gross motor activities
description: A non-academic after-school curriculum for K–1 children built from increasingly complex constructional tasks, tracing and motor precision "Paper and Pencil Activities", and gross motor games such as Red Light Green Light and Simon Says selected to exercise impulse control, sustained attention, and working memory. Activities were screened with four criteria including adaptability, complexity, trainability, and variety of materials, and were delivered by trained paraprofessionals to groups of four to seven children.
requirements: Instructors require training; implementers received 11 hours of additional curriculum training beyond a week-long behavior-management workshop
constraints: Delivered in a 45-minute block, 4 days a week, over 24 weeks of after-school programming
target_learners: kindergarten and first-grade children from low-income communities
examples: In the trial, 87 children were randomized at the school level across three Title 1 elementary schools; the intervention group received the curriculum while controls did business-as-usual activities such as girl scouts, basketball, and cooking class
key_sources: Laura L. Brock, William M. Murrah, Elizabeth A. Cottone, Andrew J. Mashburn, and David W. Grissmer. (2018). An after-school intervention targeting executive function and visuospatial skills also improves classroom behavior. International Journal of Behavioral Development, 42(5), 474–484. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025417738057

article_title: The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan
citation: Abdul Majeed Al-Tayib Umar. (2018). The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan. English Language Teaching, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p15
title: Assessment for learning as a constructive, feedback-driven process contrasted with summative assessment
description: The article defines assessment for learning (constructive assessment) as "a process used by teachers and learners during instruction that provides feedback to adjust ongoing teaching and learning to improve students' achievement of intended instructional goals". It contrasts this with summative assessment, which summarizes achievement at the end of a course for certification and is described as inherently passive. The framework centers on closing the gap between learners' current status and intended goals, with information becoming feedback only when actively used to alter that gap.
requirements: Feedback must be immediate and clearly articulated, and information must be actively used to adjust teaching or learning strategies
constraints: The article notes summative assessment remains the common university practice for certification, progression and selection
target_learning_goals: improving English for Specific Purposes achievement
closing gaps between current status and intended learning goals
examples: The experimental group's instruction used learning portfolios, classroom observations, weekly learning notebooks, quizzes after each unit, and feedback without grades
key_sources: Abdul Majeed Al-Tayib Umar. (2018). The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan. English Language Teaching, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p15

article_title: The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan
citation: Abdul Majeed Al-Tayib Umar. (2018). The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan. English Language Teaching, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p15
title: Three guiding questions of assessment for learning: where am I going, where am I now, how can I close the gap
description: Drawing on Sadler's strategies as developed by Umar, the article frames assessment for learning around three questions: "Where are you trying to go? (Identify and communicate the learning and performance goals)", "Where are you now? (Help the students to self-assess their current level of understanding)", and "How can you get there? (Help the students with strategies and skills to reach the goals)". These are rephrased from the students' point of view to involve learners from the beginning in their own learning, aiming to increase both motivation and achievement.
requirements: Learning and performance goals must be identified and communicated; students must be helped to self-assess their current understanding
key_sources: Abdul Majeed Al-Tayib Umar. (2018). The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan. English Language Teaching, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p15

article_title: The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan
citation: Abdul Majeed Al-Tayib Umar. (2018). The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan. English Language Teaching, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p15
title: Short, medium and long cycles of assessment for learning based on instruction duration
description: Citing William and Thompson (2007), the article classifies assessment for learning into three cycles by duration of instruction: "Short cycle: minute-by-minute or day-by-day assessment that concentrates on student learning within and between lessons"; medium cycle within and between instructional units covering one to four weeks; and long cycle extending between four weeks and one year. Shavelon's related continuum ranges from informal to formal, with unplanned on-the-fly assessment capitalizing on teachable moments.
requirements: Regardless of cycle or formality, the process starts with a statement of the learning goal and activities designed to reveal students' understanding of it
target_learning_goals: continuous monitoring of learning within and between lessons and units
key_sources: Abdul Majeed Al-Tayib Umar. (2018). The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan. English Language Teaching, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p15

article_title: The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan
citation: Abdul Majeed Al-Tayib Umar. (2018). The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan. English Language Teaching, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p15
title: Assessment-for-learning implementation pattern: portfolios, observations, grade-free notebooks, and unit quizzes
description: In the experimental condition the article implemented assessment for learning through a concrete toolkit: "learning portfolios, classroom observations, after class exercises and quizzes, and learning notebooks". Learning notebooks were handed in weekly containing a study summary, a plan for the next week and suggestions to the teacher, and were returned with marking that involved no grades. The instructor recorded progress and problems during observations and communicated with students in time to solve them, with group work particularly encouraged.
requirements: Instructor training: the experimental teacher received an intensive five-day training course on assessment-for-learning techniques before implementation
constraints: Some students found the grade-free marking vague and the procedures' many requirements frustrating
examples: Weekly learning notebooks with summary, next-week plan and suggestions to the teacher, marked without grades; quizzes after each unit
key_sources: Abdul Majeed Al-Tayib Umar. (2018). The Impact of Assessment for Learning on Students' Achievement in English for Specific Purposes: A Case Study of Pre-Medical Students at Khartoum University: Sudan. English Language Teaching, 11(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p15

article_title: Novel Simulation-based Awake Fiberoptic Intubation Curriculum: Pilot Study.
citation: Haas D, Fredette J, Murphy KA, Deitchman A, Anderson J, Blodgett M. (2026). Novel Simulation-based Awake Fiberoptic Intubation Curriculum: Pilot Study. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.50778
title: Novel 34-point awake fiberoptic intubation procedural checklist with instructional video
description: The authors developed a 34-maximum-point procedural checklist for awake fiberoptic intubation through literature review and iterative multidisciplinary refinement among emergency, anesthesiology, and critical care physicians, reviewed by simulation center professionals. A 40-minute instructional video covering anatomy, indications, contraindications, complications, step-by-step procedure, and troubleshooting was created based on this checklist. Preliminary validity evidence was gathered, though the authors note it remains limited.
requirements: Iterative multidisciplinary expert review to reach consensus
Review by simulation center professionals with checklist development expertise
constraints: Validity evidence is limited; no rater training, inter-rater reliability, internal consistency, or consequential validity was collected
target_learners: Emergency medicine residents and attending physicians
examples: Participants received the checklist and biweekly review reminders via a feedback platform between training and post-test
key_sources: Haas D, Fredette J, Murphy KA, Deitchman A, Anderson J, Blodgett M. (2026). Novel Simulation-based Awake Fiberoptic Intubation Curriculum: Pilot Study. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.50778

article_title: A case study: exploring the impact of 3D printed models on cognitive integration during clinical skills training.
citation: Lisk Kristina, Cheung Jeffrey JH. (2024). A case study: exploring the impact of 3D printed models on cognitive integration during clinical skills training. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.78564
title: Affordances and embodied cognition as an account of how physical models support cognitive integration
description: The authors propose that learners' cognitive integration is shaped by the affordances of the learning environment, defined as "the possibilities for action that an environment provides an individual". Introducing physical affordances such as 3D printed bones creates opportunities for learning through embodied cognition, since physical actions of the body affect mental processes. They suggest external representations encouraging physical action may support integration of visual, motor, and spatial information during clinical skills learning.
requirements: A learning environment containing physical resources, peers, and an instructor that afford particular behaviours
constraints: The authors present this as an interpretive framing of a single case study, not a tested mechanism
target_learners: health professions trainees learning procedural/clinical skills
target_learning_goals: cognitive integration of anatomical knowledge with clinical skills
examples: In the palpation laboratory, learners' bodies, peers, the instructor, and 3D printed bones all represented environmental aspects affording particular behaviours
key_sources: Lisk Kristina, Cheung Jeffrey JH. (2024). A case study: exploring the impact of 3D printed models on cognitive integration during clinical skills training. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.78564
